title: What Child Is This?
description: William Chatterton Dix's Christmas words to the old English tune Greensleeves, as Bramley and Stainer printed them in Christmas Carols New and Old, for 2 to 4 singers: verses 1 and 3, each with its own chorus, "This, this is Christ the King" and "Raise, raise, the song on high". The soprano sings the tune; the alto, tenor and bass sing the words beneath it in new parts on the book's harmony. Gentle and lilting, in a slow 6/8.

credits.words: William Chatterton Dix (as printed in Bramley and Stainer, Christmas Carols New and Old)

licence.words: public domain: William Chatterton Dix died 1898 (the book's index gives the words as "W. C. Dix")
licence.tune: public domain: traditional (the index gives the air as "Old English")
licence.arrangement: original, written for Stackapella on the chords of the book's four unsigned parts, Christmas Carols New and Old, No. XIV (the first series' own index signs no harmony for it; its music editor John Stainer died 1901 and its words editor Henry Ramsden Bramley 1917; public domain): Stainer's tune a whole tone higher; the alto, tenor and bass are new, one note a syllable, on his chords, with the bass on the chord's third at "who", "with", "is" and "to" where he has the root, and a passing seventh in the alto at "are" and "of" before the cadence; on "rest", "sweet", "King", "laud", "myrrh", "brings", "high" and "born" the alto sings in unison with the tune, as the book's alto does, and the bass takes G sharp 3 with the tenor on B3 so the trio and the four have the chord's third; on the tune's low C sharp at the end of "sleep-ing" and "own Him" (the verses) the alto holds E sharp 4, a third above the tune, with the tenor on G sharp 3, so the duet and trio have the third; breaths written in for beginners: "-ing" and "Him:" a quaver where the print has a crotchet, "Whom", "So" and "The" a semiquaver late, "keep-ing?", "en-throne Him.", "sing:", "by:" and "Ma-ry." shortened, and the last "ry!" a crotchet so the last bar and the opening pickup make one bar; accepted exceptions: the duet's unison E4 on "rest" and its seven counterparts (an alto G sharp 3 would leap a minor sixth from "laid", and an alto above the tune makes "On" a unison and the alto's line much harder); the duet's unison C sharp 4 at the chorus's "Angels sing" and "lullaby" (an alto E sharp there drops its line under the 70% easy-move rule); the alto above the tune's low C sharp at "sleep-ing" and "own Him" (rule 4: the tune's low note, so the alto takes the third above it); the soprano's low C sharp 4, four times, a semitone under the beginner range, short and at a line end (the print's B3; G minor would put the chorus's held top note on F5); the bass's two fifths, F sharp 3 to B2 and C sharp 3 to F sharp 2, in the second line of each half (iv, V, i on the roots as printed; D3 instead makes octaves with the alto); and the tenth between soprano and alto at the start of each chorus. The duet and trio go without a chord's third only on weak quavers in the second half of a bar (in the duet, the E major passing chord over G sharp on "is" in "What Child is this", the "gels" of "Angels", "Him" in "So bring Him" and "of" in "King of kings"; in the trio, the opening "What"), every dotted-crotchet beat keeping it.
licence.source: H. R. Bramley and John Stainer, Christmas Carols New and Old, first series (London: Novello, Ewer and Co.; this copy a printing of the 1870s, catalogued [187?], its title page advertising the first and second series together), No. XIV, "What Child is this?", pp. 32 and 33, in four parts in E minor, 6/8, written here a whole tone higher in F sharp minor; verse 1 as printed under the music and verse 3 as printed below it, the long s modernised; University of California Libraries copy, read from the scan at archive.org/details/christmascarolsn00staiiala/page/n37 (and n38). Compared with a later printing of the complete book (London: Novello and Company, Limited; the music editor styled "Sir John Stainer", so 1888 or later), No. 14, pp. 32 and 33, the same setting, whose index gives the words as "W. C. Dix" and the air as "Old English": Brigham Young University copy, archive.org/details/christmascarolsn00lond (page images n37, n38 and the index, n189); the first series was out in November 1867: the Musical Times of 1 December 1867 lists "Twenty Christmas Carols, Old and New" under Novello's "During the last month", its advert on p. 235 naming "14. What Child is this? ... Old English" (the story's research; the 1 November issue does not list it), so this copy is a later printing
